content: Tinea manuum is a fungal infection of the hand caused by dermatophytes, which are a group of parasitic fungi. This condition is classified as a type of dermatophytosis, commonly referred to as tinea. It is generally more aggressive than tinea pedis (athlete's foot), although it may appear similar in presentation. Symptoms of tinea manuum include itching, burning, cracking, and scaling of the skin. The infection can be transmitted through direct contact, including sexual transmission, regardless of whether symptoms are present. The diagnosis of tinea manuum is primarily clinical, based on physical examination of the affected skin. The characteristic features of the condition, such as scaling and erythema, are often sufficient for diagnosis. Visual references, such as those found in dermatology atlases, are frequently used to confirm the clinical presentation. Differential diagnosis is essential to distinguish tinea manuum from other conditions that may present with similar symptoms, such as secondary syphilis, pityriasis rosea, or eczema. These conditions can also cause rashes and scaling, necessitating careful evaluation to avoid misdiagnosis. Treatment of tinea manuum typically involves the prolonged use of topical antifungal agents, such as creams containing selenium sulfide. In more severe or refractory cases, oral antifungal medications, such as griseofulvin, may be required to achieve complete resolution of the infection.
